source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Human anchor for this angle. People cut a branch of the plan tree as soon as they meet a large loss, even when cutting is costly. A look-ahead model with a pruning term fits much better.
numbers: N=46 in 3 groups (large loss -70p n=15, -100p n=16, -140p n=15). Pruning was not reduced when costly. Look-ahead model predicted 77% of choices, Pruning+Learned model 91%. Punishments counted about 1.4x rewards. Beat SARSA by iBIC 314.
quote: they curtailed any further evaluation of a sequence as soon as they encountered a large loss.
limits: Healthy students; abstract task with 6 states; only second block analysed; no LLM data. Last 20k characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: This is the rule to test in a model: after a bad first step, stop expanding that branch. Whether it helps depends on the loss size, so a hard rule is risky.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning (J Neurosci)
finding: Replication and extension in a maze with fMRI. Aversive pruning was again large. Subgenual cingulate tracked the model's pruning measure. Insula tracked losses. The earlier depression link was not replicated; state anxiety predicted the effect.
numbers: N=40 (behaviour N=37). Correct 78% when the optimal path avoided a big loss vs 37% when it passed through one (t(36)=12.51, d=2.06). Pruning explained about 52% of suboptimal choices (range 4-93%, chance about 11%). Best model Pruning+loss iBIC 2466. Pruned trials were faster. SGC peak t(36)=3.87, pSVC=0.004.
limits: Healthy sample; timing of pruning inside the 9 s plan window unknown; behaviour and model measure correlate only r=0.63.
agent_relevance: Pruning is fast and cheap, and its cost is a skipped good branch. An agent rule must say when a fast cut is allowed.

source: Chen, Li, Cakir, Akcali, Lee, Mattar (2026) Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces Reveals Myopic Planning
finding: Four-in-a-row study with 27 LLMs. Search trees were extracted from their reasoning traces. Models search shallower than humans and their moves follow shallow nodes, not deep ones.
numbers: 27 models, round robin, 1404 games. Mean max depth 1.00-3.48 plies (1.78 +/- 0.71) vs humans 4-6. Win rate rose with breadth (beta=0.075, p=0.0025), not depth (beta=-0.015, p=0.82). A myopic model that ignores deep nodes fit moves best.
limits: One game; tree extraction used a GPT-5 judge; no loss-framing manipulation.
agent_relevance: LLMs already ignore deep futures in effect. A scaffold that widens the first-ply candidate list may help more than one that adds depth.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces (causal paragraph-pruning test)
finding: A causal test: whole paragraphs of the trace were deleted and the model re-asked for a move. Removing the chosen move's branch changed the move far more than removing other branches. Deep paragraphs added nothing.
numbers: Removing only the final decision changed the move 2.1%. Removing the chosen branch 32.0%. Removing the largest unchosen branch 1.2%. Adding back depth-1 paragraphs cut change to 4.1%; adding depth 2+ gave 3.7%.
limits: Single game; trace pruning edits text, not hidden state.
agent_relevance: Cuts made in written reasoning do change the answer. Written pruning is a real control lever for an agent.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Landmark LLM tree search with explicit pruning. An LLM evaluator labels each partial state sure, maybe or impossible and impossible branches are cut.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC(k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. CoT best-of-100 49%. About 60% of CoT samples were already wrong after the first step.
quote: around 60% of CoT samples already failed the task after generating the first step
limits: One model family; 100 tasks; ToT uses about 5.5k completion tokens per case, close to 100 CoT trials.
agent_relevance: About 60% failure after step one is the fact behind 'prune after a bad first step', but here pruning is a judged decision, not a reflex.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: crossword ablation of pruning and backtracking
finding: Removing the pruning rule in Mini Crosswords hurt. But the pruner is imperfect and also cut away some right branches.
numbers: Letter/Word/Game success: ToT 78/60/20. Without pruning 65.4/41.5/5. Without backtracking 54.6/20/5. With oracle best state 82.4/67.5/35. Ablating pruning still found the right answer in 4/20 games, 3 of which ToT with pruning missed.
limits: 20 crossword games; GPT-4 judge is noisy on rare words.
agent_relevance: A wrong pruner costs solutions. Keep a way to revive a cut branch.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: generator vs evaluator model swap
finding: Which half matters, generating thoughts or judging them. A weaker judge with a strong generator did fine. A weak generator was the bottleneck.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 74%; GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%; GPT-3.5 both 19%.
limits: Single task; GPT-3.5 needed a 3-shot proposal prompt.
agent_relevance: The pruning judge can be a cheaper model than the generator.

source: Xie et al. (2023) Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning
finding: Beam pruning guided by the model's own step-wise confidence, mixing a generation score and a correctness score. Pruning is by sampling, not hard top-k.
numbers: Gains over Codex baselines: GSM8K +6.34%, AQuA +9.56%, StrategyQA +5.46%. Mixing weight 0.5; correctness only 74.5% or generation only 77.1% vs 80.2% on GSM8K. Llama-2 beam k=10: 42.8% vs 35.7%.
limits: Correctness confidence separates right and wrong chains for arithmetic but barely for commonsense tasks.
agent_relevance: Soft, noisy pruning beat hard cuts here. Self-confidence is a usable but weak pruner outside math.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: MCTS where the LLM is both world model and reward source. Low-reward branches get less search.
numbers: Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B: RAP average success 64%; 6-step problems 42% within 20 iterations; CoT nearly zero on harder cases. About 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT.
limits: Blocksworld only for planning; rewards come from the same LLM so errors can compound.
agent_relevance: Value-driven pruning via simulated rewards helps planning; the reward is model-judged, not a loss reflex.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS over agent actions with LLM value and self-reflection after failed leaves. Reflection on a bad branch is fed back.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1 92.7 with GPT-4. WebShop score up 22.1 with GPT-3.5. HotpotQA EM tables list a LATS (DFS) variant at 0.42 and a LATS (CoT+ReAct) variant at 0.71 with GPT-3.5.
limits: Costs many more calls; external feedback (tests, environment) drives the gains.
agent_relevance: Reflect-then-retry beats a blind cut after failure when real feedback is available.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, models do not reliably fix a wrong first step. They often flip right answers to wrong ones.
numbers: With oracle labels (Table 2): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle (Table 3) gains vanish or reverse. For GSM8K with GPT-3.5, 74.7% of answers did not change after correction.
limits: Reasoning tasks, 2 rounds, a few models; later models may differ.
agent_relevance: After a bad step, 'try again' alone is not a safe fix. Use an external check before cutting or keeping a branch.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The mirror image of loss pruning. Reasoning models drop a promising line too soon and switch thoughts. This hurts accuracy.
numbers: Wrong answers use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than right ones. Over 70% of wrong responses contain at least one correct thought. TIP penalty: QwQ-32B AIME24 pass@1 38.3 to 44.1; GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8.
limits: Math and science benchmarks; gains small on strong models; penalty strength tuned on AIME22-23.
agent_relevance: Too much early abandonment is a real LLM failure. A prune-after-bad-step rule must not make this worse.

source: Hou et al. (2025) ThinkPrune: Pruning Long Chain-of-Thought of LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Training a model to prune its own long thinking with a token limit that gives zero reward when exceeded.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B average length 10,355 to 3,574 tokens with average accuracy slightly up across four math sets. AIME24 length halved for about 2% drop. QwQ-32B 8,763 to 4,494; DeepScaleR 5,914 to 3,370, each about 2% drop.
limits: Needs RL training, so it is not a scaffold. Math only.
agent_relevance: Cutting thought length pays when the cut is learned. A prompt-only scaffold cannot copy this.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Reasoning traces are stopped early when their group confidence falls below a threshold. This is a cut of a branch by an internal bad-signal.
numbers: AIME 2025 GPT-OSS-120B: pass@1 91.8%, majority vote 97.0%, DeepConf@512 99.9%. Tokens cut by up to 84.7% in online mode.
limits: Needs token probabilities; calibration varies by model.
agent_relevance: The closest working analogue of a bad-step reflex in an LLM loop. It works when the signal is calibrated.

source: Mondal, Webb, Momennejad (2025) Improving planning with LLMs: a modular agentic architecture (MAP)
finding: Brain-inspired planner with Monitor, Predictor, Evaluator, Decomposer and Orchestrator modules. The Monitor filters invalid actions, which is a pruner.
numbers: Valuepath graph task 100% solved. Tower of Hanoi 3 disks: nearly seven-fold gain over zero-shot, best of 5 runs 100%, no invalid actions proposed.
limits: Small deterministic planning tasks.
agent_relevance: Pruning illegal moves before they enter the plan is cheap and effective.

source: Mondal et al. (2025) MAP ablation: Monitor module
finding: Of all modules, ablating the Monitor (the pruner of invalid actions) hurt most.
numbers: Without the Monitor, invalid moves rose to 31% in Tower of Hanoi; other ablated variants had 0% invalid.
limits: Tower of Hanoi only.
agent_relevance: Rule-based pruning of bad branches may beat fancy judging.

source: Authors of arXiv 2605.06040 (2026) Novelty-based Tree-of-Thought Search for LLM Reasoning and Planning
finding: Prunes thought nodes that are not novel compared with earlier ones (idea from width-based classical planning). Works when tuned, collapses when not.
numbers: Blocksworld with Qwen-14B: naive prompt 3 of 50; base ToT 0 of 50, then 11 of 50 after prompt fixes; thinking mode 94% at 229k-330k tokens. Well-tuned novelty pruning cut token cost up to 20x at same performance; badly tuned gave near-zero solves and cost up over 100%.
limits: Few small benchmarks; the authors call configuration laborious and unpredictable.
agent_relevance: Pruning rules are brittle: small prompt changes flip a big saving into total failure.

source: ToolTree authors (2026) ToolTree: Efficient LLM Agent Tool Planning via Dual-Feedback MCTS and Bidirectional Pruning (ICLR 2026)
finding: Agent tool planning with pre-pruning (no child if score is below a threshold before running a tool) and post-pruning (after a bad result, the edge is marked non-viable).
numbers: Average gain about 10 percent over the best prior planner on 4 benchmarks. GTA with GPT-4o average 66.95. Open tool tasks with GPT-4o-mini: PathVQA +22.22 and Game-of-24 +16.83 points over few-shot.
limits: Thresholds are LLM-scored; baselines run by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest published form of 'prune after a bad step' in an LLM agent: post-pruning after observed failure. Needs tuned thresholds.

source: Coda-Forno, Witte, Jagadish, Binz, Akata, Schulz (2024) Inducing anxiety in large language models can induce bias
finding: Anxiety-inducing prompts raise the anxiety score of most models and raise biased answers. Huys linked pruning to mood; here mood is manipulated by prompt text.
numbers: 12 LLMs tested, 6 passed robustness checks. Anxiety prompt raised STICSA vs neutral for all six (all t>3.36, p<.01). Biased answers rose with preprompt STICSA (beta=0.08, p=.02); any preprompt raised bias vs none (anxious beta=0.62 p=.004; neutral 0.71 p=.001). GPT-4 and Claude-1 showed no such effect and were less than half as biased.
limits: Bias benchmark, not planning; two non-RLHF models did not respond.
agent_relevance: Mood text in a prompt can shift an LLM. Loss-coloured wording might move how it prunes; this is untested.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara, Chen (2024) Decision-Making Behavior Evaluation Framework for LLMs under Uncertain Context
finding: Prospect-theory estimates for three LLMs. All were risk averse and loss averse, but the size differed by model.
numbers: ChatGPT-4.0-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.0-pro, 300 repeated lottery prompts each. All risk-averse (mean above 0, min above 0). ChatGPT showed the lowest loss aversion, Claude the highest. ChatGPT probability-weighting parameter above 1, unlike humans.
limits: One-shot lotteries, no sequential planning; older model versions.
agent_relevance: LLMs carry loss weights, so a loss-triggered cut is plausible, but strength varies by model. Test per model.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Adding emotional lines to a prompt changes accuracy. Prompt affect is a real lever.
numbers: Relative gain 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench; human study 10.9% average gain on generative tasks.
limits: Positive emotional lines only; no loss or negative framing.
agent_relevance: Affect text in a scaffold matters; test whether loss-coloured wording changes branch choices.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation
finding: Plain LLMs are poor planners, which is why search and pruning scaffolds were built.
numbers: Autonomous plan generation averaged about 3% success; preliminary human baseline 78% for plan generation and 70% for optimal planning.
limits: Older models (GPT-3 class, BLOOM, Instruct-GPT).
agent_relevance: Pruning must sit around the model, not inside its first guess.

source: Knuth and Moore (1975) An analysis of alpha-beta pruning
finding: Classic AI result. Alpha-beta cuts branches that cannot change the minimax value, so it is exact pruning.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not read this session.
limits: Not opened this session; stated from standard knowledge.
agent_relevance: Exact pruning is safe. A loss-triggered cut is not exact, which is why it can fail.

source: Buro (1999) ProbCut: forward pruning in game-tree search
finding: Heuristic forward pruning: cut a branch when a shallow search says it is probably outside the window. It trades a small error rate for depth.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not read this session.
limits: Not opened this session; stated from standard knowledge.
agent_relevance: A cut guided by a shallow look resembles what people do: cheap, usually fine, sometimes wrong.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies (PNAS)
finding: Follow-up: people also chunk plans as well as prune. Page returned 403 this session.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Pruning is one of several cost-saving planning moves; an agent may also need chunking.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: Resource-rational model of planning that chooses where to spend thought. Page needed login this session.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for when cutting is worth it: only when thinking costs more than the expected gain.
